title: What is this?
goal: Point at things near and far, name their colors, and form plurals with a single letter — without ever dealing with articles or gender.
bekal: tell *tämä*, *tuo*, and *se* apart by their distance from the speaker
make plurals with the ending **-t** and make the adjective change along with them
name about twenty everyday objects and their colors

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Uusi huone
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved into a dorm room in Espoo. Aino comes over to help him settle in.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Oho, huone on iso! Mikä tuo on?
lines.id: Wow, the room is big! What's that?
lines.literal: oh, room is big! what that-over-there is?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tuo on minun uusi pöytä. Ja tämä on tuoli.
lines.id: That's my new desk. And this is the chair.
lines.literal: that-over-there is my new table. and this is chair.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Pöytä on tosi kaunis. Onko se puuta?
lines.id: The desk is really beautiful. Is it wood?
lines.literal: table is really beautiful. is-? it wood-partitive?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: On. Se on vanha, mutta se on hyvä.
lines.id: Yes. It's old, but it's good.
lines.literal: is. it is old, but it is good.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ne ovat kirjoja. Suomen kirjat ovat tuossa, ja nämä ovat sanakirjat.
lines.id: They're books. The Finnish books are over there, and these are the dictionaries.
lines.literal: they are books-partitive. Finnish's books are in-that, and these are dictionaries.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: One is Finnish–English, the other is Finnish–Indonesian.

lines.speaker: Aino:
lines.text: Fiksua! Entä tuo sininen laukku — onko se sinun?
lines.id: Smart! And that blue bag — is it yours?
lines.literal: smart! and that-over-there blue bag — is-? it yours?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ei ole. Se on Marekin. Minun laukku on musta.
lines.id: No. It's Marek's. My bag is the black one.
lines.literal: not is. it is Marek's. my bag is black.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voi ei. En tiedä! Ehkä ne ovat pöydällä.
lines.id: Oh no. I don't know! Maybe they're on the desk.
lines.literal: oh no. not-I know! maybe they are on-table.

notes: **Three distances, not two.** English has "this" and "that"; Finnish has three levels — *tämä* (near the speaker), *tuo* (away from both of you, but visible), *se* (already mentioned, or near the listener). In practice *se* is also what you use to refer back to something just mentioned, exactly like "it" in "it's nice".

**Ne ovat kirjoja** uses a form you haven't learned yet.** *Kirjoja* is the **partitive plural** — used when you mean "some books" with no exact number. Compare *sanakirjat* in the same line: that's the ordinary plural, because the dictionaries are clearly both of them. For now, just feel the difference; the rule is covered in Unit 11.

**Onko se puuta?** literally "is it wood-partitive". Materials always take the partitive, because the object is made **of some** of the material, not of all the wood in the world. *Se on puuta* (made of wood), *se on metallia* (of metal), *se on muovia* (of plastic).

**On on its own means "yes".** Look at line 4: the question *Onko se puuta?* is answered *On.* Finnish often answers a question by **repeating the verb**, not with *kyllä*. To say no: *Ei ole.* This habit sounds very Finnish, and copying it makes your Finnish instantly more natural.

**Marekin** — possession is made with the ending **-n**. *Marek* → *Marekin laukku* (Marek's bag), *Aino* → *Ainon kirja*. The same ending that makes *minun* from *minä*. We'll cover it fully in the next unit.
**Adjectives go in front, just as in English.** *Sininen laukku*, *musta laukku*, *uusi pöytä* — not "laukku sininen". Good news: here your English instincts are exactly right.

grammars.title: Tämä, tuo, se — and their plurals
body: Six words that cover all pointing. Note that the plurals aren't made by adding *-t* but are separate forms you have to memorize — one of the few places in Finnish that truly calls for rote learning.

rows: it, that (already mentioned; near the listener)

after: *Mikä tämä on?* — "what's this?" The answer almost always uses *se*, not *tämä* again: *Se on kirja.* Repeating *tämä* sounds like a small child pointing at things.
The plurals need a plural verb too: *tämä **on*** but *nämä **ovat***. English does this too (*is/are*), so it should feel familiar.

⚠️ In everyday speech Finns use *se* and *ne* for almost everything, people included — *se sanoi* (he/she said). It really is used, but it sounds very casual; don't copy it in letters or with people you don't know well.

grammars.title: Plurals with -t, and adjectives that follow along
body: Making a plural is as easy as adding one letter. What takes a new habit is that **the adjective changes too** — something that never happens in English.
after: **The adjective takes exactly the same ending as its noun.** *Iso talo → isot talot*. Once this pattern sinks in, it also holds for the fourteen other endings you'll learn later — the adjective always copies its noun, no exceptions. A far tidier deal than German or French.
⚠️ Notice *pöytä → pöydät* and *kauppa → kaupat*: the consonant weakens when *-t* is attached. By contrast, *kirja → kirjat* doesn't change, because there's no *k*, *p*, or *t* to weaken.

⚠️ Words ending in *-nen* (*ihminen*, *punainen*, *nainen*) first change their ending to *-se-*: *ihminen → ihmiset*, *punainen → punaiset*. This group is huge in Finnish, so the pattern pays off fast.

blocks.text: *Tietokone* (computer) literally means "knowledge machine" — *tieto* (knowledge) + *kone* (machine). Finnish loves building new words from its own material instead of borrowing: *puhelin* (phone) from *puhua* (speak), *jääkaappi* (fridge) from *jää* (ice) + *kaappi* (cupboard). This habit helps you guess the meaning of long words you've never seen.

Six of the eleven colors above end in *-nen*, and that's no accident: *-nen* is the most productive adjective-forming ending in Finnish. If you meet an unfamiliar word ending in *-nen*, your best bet is that it's an adjective.

*Vaalea* means "light" and *tumma* means "dark". Both go in front of a color with the possessive ending: *vaaleanpunainen* (pink, literally "light's red"), *tummansininen* (dark blue). Note that they fuse into a single word.

blocks.title: Asking about color
items: *Minkä värinen tämä on?* — "What color is this?" Literally "what's colored this is".
*Se on sininen.* — "It's blue." For plurals: *Ne ovat sinisiä* — note that the plural in this position takes the partitive, just like *Ne ovat kirjoja* in the dialogue.
The table is big and beautiful.
This is a dictionary, and that's a notebook.
